claim: When a Kinesis data stream is the source, Kinesis Data Streams encrypts the data with a KMS key before storing it and decrypts it when the Firehose stream reads it. Firehose buffers the data in memory and delivers it without storing unencrypted data at rest.
question: How is data encrypted when the source of a Firehose stream is a Kinesis data stream?

values.display: Kinesis Data Streams encrypts your data using an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key
without storing the unencrypted data at rest

evidence.quote: When your Firehose stream reads the data from your data stream, Kinesis Data Streams first decrypts the data and then sends it to Amazon Data Firehose. Amazon Data Firehose buffers the data in memory based on the buffering hints that you specify. It then delivers it to your destinations without storing the unencrypted data at rest.
When you send data from your data producers to your data stream, Kinesis Data Streams encrypts your data using an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key before storing the data at rest.

claim: For data sent with PutRecord, PutRecordBatch, AWS IoT, CloudWatch Logs or CloudWatch Events, you can turn on Firehose server-side encryption with the StartDeliveryStreamEncryption operation. You can also enable it when you create the Firehose stream.

values.display: StartDeliveryStreamEncryption
enable SSE when you create the Firehose stream

qualifiers.scope: Direct PUT and other non-Kinesis sources

evidence.quote: If you send data to your Firehose stream using [PutRecord](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/firehose/latest/APIReference/API_PutRecord.html) or [PutRecordBatch](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/firehose/latest/APIReference/API_PutRecordBatch.html), or if you send the data using AWS IoT, Amazon CloudWatch Logs, or CloudWatch Events, you can turn on server-side encryption by using the [StartDeliveryStreamEncryption](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/firehose/latest/APIReference/API_StartDeliveryStreamEncryption.html) operation.
You can also enable SSE when you create the Firehose stream.

claim: Amazon MSK Replicator is a fully managed feature that replicates data across Amazon MSK clusters in different or the same AWS Region. When replicating between MSK clusters, the source and target clusters must be in the same AWS account.

MSK Replicator also supports data replication from self-managed Apache Kafka clusters (including on-premises, self-hosted on AWS, or other cloud providers) to Amazon MSK Provisioned clusters. Both the source and target clusters must be in the same AWS account when replicating between MSK clusters.

claim: MSK Replicator replicates data and consumer group offsets between MSK clusters asynchronously, and also the Kafka metadata such as topic configurations and ACLs. If an unexpected event occurs in a Region, you can fail over to the other Region and resume processing.

evidence.quote: MSK Replicator also replicates the necessary Kafka metadata including topic configurations, Access Control Lists (ACLs), and consumer group offsets. If an unexpected event occurs in a Region, you can failover to the other AWS Region and seamlessly resume processing.

MSK Replicator provides automatic asynchronous replication of data and consumer group offsets between MSK clusters, eliminating the need to write custom code, manage infrastructure, or setting up cross-region networking.

For cross-account replication between Amazon MSK clusters, you must use Apache MirrorMaker 2.0.

claim: The Lambda integration connects an Amazon MSK cluster to a Lambda function with an event source mapping that constantly polls the topic for messages with an Event Poller. The mapping checks the message backlog with the OffsetLag metric and auto-scales Event Pollers.
question: How does Lambda read messages from an Amazon MSK topic?

values.display: Event Source Mapping (ESM) which constantly polls for messages in your topic
auto-scales Event Pollers

evidence.quote: The Lambda integration connects your Amazon MSK cluster to the selected Lambda function, using an Event Source Mapping (ESM) which constantly polls for messages in your topic using a resource called Event Poller.

The ESM evaluates the message backlog – using the [OffsetLag metric](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/offset-lag-metric-for-amazon-msk-as-an-event-source-for-lambda/) – for all partitions in the topic, and auto-scales Event Pollers to process messages efficiently.
